title: Gujarat Bans Analogue Paneer and Dairy Substitutes in Widening Food Safety Crackdown
excerpt: The western Indian state joins a national push to pull cheap vegetable-fat imitations off menus and store shelves, with over 2,500 eateries inspected and hundreds of kilograms of substandard food destroyed.
body:
• Gujarat has banned the sale and labeling of analogue paneer, cheese, and butter, requiring all food establishments to disclose whether they use dairy or vegetable-fat substitutes.
  • India's food regulator FSSAI has moved to prohibit analogue paneer nationally, with about 1,000 existing license holders given a transition period to exit the market.
  • Real dairy paneer retails at roughly ₹460 per kg while analogue versions sell for ₹250–300 per kg, with about 90% of India's paneer traded in the unregulated loose market.
  • Gujarat's enforcement drives have inspected 2,527 food establishments, destroyed 703 kg of substandard food, and sealed 18 businesses since April.

Gujarat has banned the manufacture and sale of analogue paneer, cheese, and butter, becoming the latest Indian state to crack down on cheap vegetable-fat imitations that regulators say mislead consumers and undermine the nutritional integrity of a staple protein source for hundreds of millions of Indians.

The move follows Maharashtra's ban on analogue dairy products earlier this year and aligns with a national-level push by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to eliminate an entire category of non-standardized dairy substitutes from the market.

What Is Analogue Paneer?

Analogue paneer is manufactured from vegetable oils — typically palm or palmolein oil — blended with milk solids, starch, and emulsifiers to mimic the taste, texture, and appearance of genuine dairy paneer. The products are significantly cheaper to produce, retailing at ₹250–300 per kg compared with ₹460 for branded dairy paneer from companies like Amul or Mother Dairy.

The price gap has created a massive market for substitutes, particularly in the unregulated "loose" segment that accounts for roughly 90% of all paneer sold in India. Authorities say unscrupulous vendors purchase analogue paneer in bulk and sell it as genuine product — something ordinary buyers cannot detect, as the imitation closely mimics real paneer's look and feel.

"The big question is why fake or duplicate products made with palmolein oil are legally allowed to use dairy names like cheese or paneer. It's like allowing gold-polished brass or aluminium jewellery to use the BIS hallmark logo."

— R.S. Sodhi, former Managing Director, Amul (GCMMF)

Gujarat's Enforcement Campaign

Gujarat's Food and Drugs Control Administration (FDCA) has been conducting intensive enforcement drives since issuing a directive on April 4 requiring all food business operators to clearly disclose whether they use milk paneer or analogue substitutes. A statewide "mega special drive" between April 4 and 9 inspected 2,527 establishments including restaurants, dhabas, and street food units.

During the campaign, authorities issued 270 notices for violations, sealed or closed 18 establishments, collected penalties totalling ₹2,84,300, and destroyed 703 kg of food deemed unfit for consumption. Food Safety Vans inspected 659 units and conducted on-the-spot testing of 679 samples.

Gujarat Health Minister Praful Pansheriya said eateries must clearly indicate the type of paneer being served, adding that failure to do so amounts to misleading consumers. Businesses can no longer present analogue products simply as "paneer" — they must label them as "analogue" or "vegetable-fat paneer alternative" on menus and display boards.

A National Ban Takes Shape

Gujarat's state-level action mirrors a broader national shift. The FSSAI's Central Advisory Committee finalized a proposal in October 2025 — formally adopted on March 2, 2026 — to ban analogue paneer outright across India. The plan involves a transition period for approximately 1,000 current license holders to remove their products from the market.

India's food safety rules had permitted dairy analogues but set no quality standards for them, creating a regulatory grey zone. The FSSAI is now moving to eliminate the category entirely rather than attempt to enforce standards on products it considers nutritionally deficient.

The regulator is deploying two scientific markers for detection: fatty acid profiling and the beta-sitosterol test. Beta-sitosterol, a plant sterol present in vegetable oils but virtually absent in pure milk fat, flags adulteration when it exceeds 7 parts per million.

Industry Support, Consumer Impact

"As one of India's leading dairy brands, we believe this move will set a strong precedent for the industry and further strengthen trust in the country's dairy ecosystem," said Jayatheertha Chary, managing director of Mother Dairy.

Health experts echo the concern. Dr. Rajeev Jayadevan, a public health specialist and former president of the Indian Medical Association (Cochin), warned that long-term consumption of analogue paneer is unhealthy "not only because of the fats but also the emulsifiers that can disrupt healthy gut bacteria."

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indians abroad who regularly consume paneer — one of the most ubiquitous ingredients in Indian vegetarian cooking — the crackdown highlights a food safety gap that has persisted for years. NRIs visiting India or purchasing paneer from Indian grocery stores internationally may want to verify sourcing, particularly for unbranded loose products. The regulatory push could also accelerate consolidation in India's fragmented dairy sector, potentially benefiting branded players whose products are already available in diaspora markets.
nri_angle: NRIs who regularly consume paneer should verify sourcing, especially unbranded loose products; the crackdown highlights a food safety gap in India that affects diaspora visits and imports.
